title: My husband fought me for everything in the divorce. The house, the cars, the camper we used maybe twice. By the end I just wanted it over, so I let him have it. – MP STORY
excerpt: My husband fought me for everything.Not just the things that mattered.Everything.The house.Both cars.The camper we had used exactly twice.The dining table my parents had helped us buy when we were newly married.
author: admin

blocks.text: My husband fought me for everything.Not just the things that mattered.Everything.The house.Both cars.The camper we had used exactly twice.The dining table my parents had helped us buy when we were newly married.
Even the ridiculous stainless-steel grill he had insisted on purchasing three summers earlier and then complained about every time he had to clean it.
By the end of the divorce, I was so exhausted that I stopped caring who won.

He wanted me tired.He wanted me overwhelmed.He wanted me to look across the conference table at all the paperwork and think, Fine. Take it. Just leave me alone.And eventually, I did.”Keep the house,” I told him.
My attorney looked at me.”Are you sure, Laura?””No,” I said. “But I’m sure I don’t want to spend another six months fighting over bricks and furniture.”
Daniel smiled when he heard.Not a big smile.
Just that small, satisfied curl of his mouth I had spent fifteen years learning to hate.
He got the house.The cars.The camper.Most of the furniture.I took my clothes, my personal things, and a few pieces of furniture that had belonged to my mother.
There was only one thing Daniel didn’t bother fighting me for.
It was a heavy, dark piece of furniture with clawed feet, scratched wood, and a cloudy mirror that made everyone look slightly haunted.
The vanity had sat in Daniel’s grandmother’s hallway for as long as he could remember.
When she died, Daniel’s mother had insisted someone keep it.
And somehow, after we got married, it ended up in our house.
For years it sat in one room or another, collecting dust, laundry, unopened mail, and occasionally Daniel’s forgotten socks.
When the movers came during the divorce, I pointed at it.
“You can have the ugly thing,” he said. “Nobody wants it.”
But Daniel had just given me the only thing he should have fought to keep.
For nearly a year, the vanity sat in the spare room of my small apartment.
I had moved from a four-bedroom house into a two-bedroom place on the other side of town.
Then I started to appreciate the silence.
No one reminding me that I was “lucky” Daniel had stayed with me after I stopped working full-time to help him through his father’s illness.
I started sleeping through the night again.
I bought one plate at a time because I didn’t need twelve.
I learned that a small apartment could feel more like home than a big house ever had.
And every time I looked at it, I remembered Daniel laughing.
So one Saturday afternoon, I decided to sell it.
She said she could come the next morning.
That was when I decided to clean it out.
The top drawers were empty except for dust.
The bottom drawer had an old bobby pin and something that looked like it might once have been a peppermint.
Finally, I grabbed a flashlight and got down on the floor.
There was a narrow gap behind the drawer.
Then my fingertips touched something smooth.
Maybe because old furniture is supposed to contain dust.
The edge of whatever it was was covered in brittle yellow tape.
On the front, written in faded blue ink, were three words.
I told myself it was probably an old letter.
Something sentimental Daniel’s grandmother had forgotten.
Inside were several documents tied together with a red ribbon.
A small brass key with a number stamped into it.
The first document was yellowed around the edges.
But the name at the top was unmistakable.
The account balance made me sit down on the floor.
Margaret Bennett had lived in a modest little house.
She wore the same cardigan every Christmas.
She complained about expensive restaurants.
She gave the grandchildren twenty-dollar bills in birthday cards.
Daniel had always described her as “comfortable, but nothing special.”
Daniel, if you are reading this, then I have either failed to tell you the truth myself, or someone has made sure you never learned it.
Margaret had written about Daniel’s grandfather.
About a business nobody in the family talked about.
And then I reached the part that changed everything.
Twenty-three years earlier, Daniel’s grandfather had died suddenly.
Before his death, he had owned a small parcel of land outside town.
According to Daniel, his grandmother had sold it years ago for almost nothing.
But the documents told a different story.
A natural gas company had signed a long-term agreement.
The payments had been placed into a trust.
